## Overview {#sec-overview}

The 111 simulation spent most of its time in pandas, not in the simulation. For every new caller, every step of a patient's journey and every result row, it built or filtered a small DataFrame to look up a value that never changes during a run. Three commits move that work to the two ends of a run. Lookups are built once, as lists, dicts and a `Counter`, when the model starts. DataFrames are assembled once, when results are written. Seeded output is byte-identical. Timed back to back, a 3-day run went from 31.3s to 0.2s.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
- **Scope**: `4188308..8a5fc92`: commits `364702f` (result rows), `f86edd2` (arrival rates) and `8a5fc92` (per-step and per-caller lookups), on branch `add-codebase-tutorial`.
- **Files**: `hsm.py`, `transitions.py`, `caller.py`, `call_dispositions.py`. No inputs, outputs or settings changed.
- **Level**: intermediate. Key excerpts only; every changed line is toured in `kompreni/walkthroughs/2026-11-26-faster-simulation-without-pandas-hot-loops.qmd`.
- **After reading** you will know where the time went, how each hot path works now, why the output stays identical, and how to add a lookup without bringing the slowness back.
:::

## The problem {#sec-problem}

The regression suite, three short seeded simulations, took about 45-50s, and app runs of a week or more took much longer *(observed in the session that made these commits)*. A profile of one short run, about 650 callers, showed where the time went *(observed)*:

- **Storing result rows: 46%.** 6.2s of a 13.4s profiled run, all in `pd.concat`.
- **Generating callers: 4.3s.** Almost all of it three `DataFrame.query()` calls per caller.
- **Per-step lookups: about 1.4s.** A row-by-row `apply` for the network graph, and a filter for the next destination.
- **Sampling with scipy: about 0.1s.** This was the cost expected to matter most, and it barely registered.

Result rows were the worst offender, because their cost grows with the square of the run's length: each row rebuilt the whole results table.

## Before {#sec-before}

**Running example.** In the regression test's default case (seed 42, quarterly transitions, base arrivals, no what-if), patient 4 arrives at minute 76.45: 01:16 on Friday 1 January 2021, quarter 1. They are allocated GP surgery `B83054`, get the outcome `contact_12` with no timely GP contact, and their first step goes from the index 111 call (`Index_IUC`) to another 111 contact (`IUC`). The first two rows of `tests/fixtures/regression/qtr_base_no_whatif/all_results.csv` record this.

At `4188308`, that one arrival and first step took about a dozen pandas operations:
- four boolean masks in `Caller.__init__` (`caller.py:29-36@4188308`);
- three `.query()` calls for the arrival rates at (hour 1, weekday 1, quarter 1) (`hsm.py:189-196@4188308`);
- one filter of the transition table for (`Index_IUC`, quarter 1) (`transitions.py:56-70@4188308`);
- an `apply` over all 42 network rows, to add 1 to one cell (`hsm.py:296@4188308`);
- two `pd.concat` calls for the patient's two result rows, each copying every row stored so far (`hsm.py:379-386@4188308`).

## Concepts used here {#sec-concepts}

::: {.callout-tip title="Why the same random choices come out"}
`random.choices(items, weights=w)` builds cumulative weights and picks with one random number. The same items, in the same order, with the same weights, give the same pick. So replacing a pandas Series with a plain list of the same values, in the same order, changes nothing about which destination, disposition or surgery is chosen. The new lookups keep CSV row order for this reason (`transitions.py:36-41`).
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="The fixed cost of each pandas call"}
Filtering, querying or concatenating a DataFrame has a large fixed cost per call: it builds new index and column objects and allocates memory. A dict lookup costs a tiny fraction of that. In a loop that runs thousands of times, the fixed cost dominates.
:::

## What changed {#sec-what-changed}

### Storing results: a list, then one concat (`364702f`) {#sec-what-results}

`store_patient_results` appends each row to `self.results_rows` (`hsm.py:406`). `write_all_results` builds the table once, by concatenating all the rows onto the same empty `results_df` the old code started from (`hsm.py:418`). That single concat reproduces the old CSV exactly, including column order and whole numbers written as `1.0`, which the Sankey preparation in `utilities.py:208` relies on.

### Arrival rates: one dict lookup per caller (`f86edd2`) {#sec-what-arrivals}

`HSM.__init__` indexes `inter_arrival_times.csv` once, by (hour, weekday flag, quarter), into `self.interarrival_lookup` (`hsm.py:112-119`). All 192 keys are unique, so a lookup returns exactly the row `.query()` found. The start date is parsed once (`hsm.py:122`).

### Per-step and per-caller lookups (`8a5fc92`) {#sec-what-steps}

- **Next destination:** `Transitions.__init__` groups the transition table once into destination and weight lists per step and quarter, in CSV order (`transitions.py:32-41`). `next_destination` looks them up.
- **Network graph:** each step adds 1 to a `Counter` (`hsm.py:318`), and the network table's weights are filled from it once, when results are written (`hsm.py:429-432`).
- **ED attendances:** `avoidable_ed_admission` reads a dict (`transitions.py:193`).
- **New callers:** disposition draws use lists and dicts built in `CallDispositions` (`call_dispositions.py:34-39`, `caller.py:29-36`). The GP surgery draw uses lists built in `HSM.__init__` (`hsm.py:63-65`).

## How it works now {#sec-how-it-works-now}

Patient 4 again, through the three places where the most time went. In each pair, the tinted lines are what the change touched: yellow for changed, green for added, red for removed.

**Storing a result row.** Patient 4's two rows are now each a list append.

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Before
```{.python .numberLines startFrom="379" removed="381,383-386" filename="hsm.py:379-386@4188308"}
    def store_patient_results(self, results: dict) -> None:
        """
            Adds a row of data to the Class' `result_df` dataframe
        """

        df_dictionary = pd.DataFrame([results])  # <1>

        self.results_df = pd.concat([self.results_df, df_dictionary], ignore_index=True)  # <1>
```
1. A one-row DataFrame, then a concat that copies every row stored so far: quadratic in run length.

#### After
```{.python .numberLines startFrom="401" added="403-404,406" filename="hsm.py:401-406"}
    def store_patient_results(self, results: dict) -> None:
        """
            Stores a row of results. Rows are collected in a list because concatenating
            a DataFrame per row copies every earlier row each time (quadratic in run length).
        """
        self.results_rows.append(results)  # <1>
```
1. Constant time. The rows become a DataFrame once, in `write_all_results` (@sec-what-results).
:::

**Looking up the arrival rates.** For patient 4 the key is `(1, 1, 1)`: 01:00, a weekday, quarter 1.

## How the pieces fit together {#sec-fit}

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-hot-loops
%%| fig-cap: "Lookups are built once; the hot loops only read them and append"
flowchart LR
  subgraph startup ["Built once"]
    CD["CallDispositions: dx lists and dicts"]
    HI["HSM.__init__: surgeries, arrival rates, start date"]
    TI["Transitions.__init__: destinations, avoidable probabilities"]
  end
  subgraph loops ["Run thousands of times"]
    A["new caller: Caller and generate_111_calls"]
    S["each step: next_destination and transition count"]
    R["each result row: list append"]
  end
  CD --> A
  HI --> A
  TI --> S
  A --> S --> R
  R --> W["write_all_results: one concat, one weight fill"]
  S --> W
```

Each lookup is built where its table was already loaded (@fig-hot-loops). The hot loops only read dicts and lists, and append to a list or a `Counter`. All DataFrame work moves to the two ends of a run. Nothing outside the model changed: `runSim` still builds an `HSM` and calls `run()`, and the CSVs the Dash app reads are identical.

## Decisions and alternatives {#sec-decisions}

- **Byte-identical output as a hard requirement** *(stated in the session that made the commits)*. The seeded regression test could then prove each step. Every detail follows from it: same row order, same weights, same draws, the same final concat.
- **Concatenating onto the empty `results_df`** rather than writing `pd.DataFrame(rows)` directly *(code: the comment at `hsm.py:415-417`)*. It keeps the column order and float formatting that `utilities.py:208` depends on.
- **Batched scipy sampling was dropped** *(stated, observed)*. The profile showed sampling took about 1% of the run. Batching would also have changed the order of random draws, so the fixtures would have needed regenerating.
- **One hotspot per commit:** the largest remaining hotspot, tested and benchmarked before the next *(commit messages `364702f`, `f86edd2`, `8a5fc92`; stated)*.
- **Left alone:** pure-Python date handling (now negligible), closing the process pool, and the slow `tree` transitions, which reload a pickled model on every step *(stated)*.

## Verification {#sec-verification}

No tests were added in this range, and there's no PR, so there are no CI results. These commits were made in one working session, and these checks were run there *(observed)*:

- **Regression test:** `pytest` passed (4 passed) after each commit, and after each of `8a5fc92`'s three steps. The suite's runtime fell from about 45-50s to 1.8s.
- **Settings the test doesn't cover:** the `max` and `mean` arrival options and the `tree` transitions gave identical output before and after `8a5fc92`.
- **Benchmarks:** a seeded 3-day run, with each version exported from its commit and timed back to back. In one round: original 10.9s, after `364702f` 5.6s, after `f86edd2` 2.5s. In another, slower round: original 31.3s, after `f86edd2` 4.7s, after `8a5fc92` 0.2s. The output hash was identical every time.

**Gaps:** nothing was run through the Dash app's process pool, or on Linux, and no long runs (such as 365 days) were timed.

## Limitations and knock-on effects {#sec-limitations}

- **Lookups are snapshots taken at start-up.** Code that later edited a source DataFrame during a run would no longer affect the simulation *(code)*. Nothing does this today.
- **Results are only filled in at the end.** `results_df` and the network weights are only filled in `write_all_results`. During a run, the data lives in `results_rows` and `transition_counts`.
- **A missing key now raises `KeyError`,** instead of failing on an empty selection *(inferred)*.
- **`364702f`'s commit message overstates its own speed-up.** It says 34.5s → 14.7s, measured while the machine was busier. Back to back, the same versions took 10.9s and 5.6s.
- **The arrival cut-off bug remains,** and is still pinned by the regression test (`hsm.py:185-186`).

## Check your understanding {#sec-quiz}

**1. For patient 4's first step, which key does `next_destination` look up, and which weights does it pass to `random.choices`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The key `('Index_IUC', 1)`, because the transitions are quarterly and it is quarter 1. Patient 4 had no timely GP contact, so the "no" weights are used. See @sec-how-it-works-now.
:::

**2. Halfway through a run, what does `network_df`'s `weight` column contain?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
All zeros, as `create_network_df` made it. During the run, the counts go only into `self.transition_counts`. The column is filled from them in `write_all_results`. See @sec-what-steps.
:::

**3. Why does `write_all_results` concatenate onto the empty `results_df` instead of writing `pd.DataFrame(self.results_rows)` directly?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
To keep the old CSV format exactly: the template's column order, and float dtypes that write whole numbers as `1.0`. The Sankey preparation relies on that format, and the regression test checks it byte for byte. See @sec-what-results.
:::

## Worth remembering {#sec-remember}

- In this model, never filter, query, `apply` or concatenate a DataFrame per caller, step or result row. Build a dict or list in an `__init__`, and read it in the loop.
- To keep seeded output identical, a lookup must give the same values, in the same order, as the code it replaces.
- After any change to the model, run `pytest`. It takes under 2 seconds now.

## Useful elsewhere {#sec-useful}

- **Gotcha: `pd.concat` in a loop is quadratic (pandas 1.4.4).** Each call copies every row already in the frame. Collect dicts in a list and build the DataFrame once. Here that alone halved a 3-day run (@sec-what-results) *(observed)*.
- **Gotcha: an empty DataFrame decides the dtypes of what you concatenate onto it (pandas 1.4.4).** Integer rows concatenated onto empty float columns are written as `1.0`, and missing columns are added at the end. A faster rewrite must keep that step if the exact output matters (@sec-what-results) *(observed in the saved CSVs)*.
- **Pattern: precompute lookups for a simulation's hot loop.** Small tables queried per event belong in dicts keyed by exactly what the loop knows. The cost: a little start-up time, and lookups that don't follow later edits to the DataFrame (@sec-what-steps) *(observed)*.
- **Technique: profile before optimising.** The suspected hotspot, scipy sampling, took about 1% of the run, so the riskiest planned change was dropped (@sec-decisions) *(observed)*.
